claims.quote_britannica: For Juno ha-ving decided Jupiter, in scaling Enulflets to be born before Hercules, Jupiter expelled his retirement on Ates, as the author of that miichief; and threw her headlong from heaven to earth, featuring the floodal never return children again
claims.quote_wikipedia: According to Agamemnon, when Alcmene was about to give birth to Zeus's son Heracles, Zeus, in his great pride, boasted that on that day would be born a man, of Zeus's blood, who would be king of the Argives. But Hera tricked Zeus into swearing an unbreakable oath such that whatever man, of Zeus's blood, born that day would be king. Then Hera delayed the birth of Heracles, and caused Eurystheus, the great-grandson of Zeus, to be born prematurely, and thus Heracles lost the birthright Zeus had intended for him.

claims.quote_wikipedia: So said he, and whirling her in his hand flung her from the starry heaven, and quickly she came to the tilled fields of men.

claims.claim: The name of the goddess comes from a Greek word meaning to hurt
claims.quote_britannica: The name of the goddels comes from stars, men, to hart.
claims.quote_wikipedia: The meaning of her name, the Greek word atē (ἄτη), is difficult to define. Atē is a verbal noun of the verb aáō (ἀάω). According to The Cambridge Greek Lexicon, aáō means to "lead astray", "befuddle", "blind", or "delude", while ἄτη can mean: (1) the state of "delusion, infatuation (inflicted on a person's mind by a god, esp Zeus)", (2) "reckless behavior... recklessness, folly", and (3) "ruin, calamity, harm".

wiki_only_topics.topic: Hesiod's account of Ate as daughter of Eris and her siblings
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: Hesiod presented Ate as one of the several offspring of Eris, all of whom were personifications representing some of the many harms which can arise out of discord and strife. Hesiod particular associates Ate with her sister Dysnomia (Lawlessness). While listing the children of Eris, he lists both on the same line (230) of his Theogony and says they are "much like one another".

wiki_only_topics.topic: Ate's role in Homer's Iliad, including the parable of Prayers and Book 19 speech
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: In Homer, atē is something inflicted by the gods; it causes delusion, then folly, then disaster. Ate, as the personification of atē, receives its fullest development in Homer 's Iliad, his epic poem about the Trojan War. However, to what extent Homer may have considered Ate to be an actual divinity as opposed to a mere allegory is unclear.

wiki_only_topics.topic: Ate in Aeschylus's Oresteia and connection to Helen and Clytemnestra
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: Ate also appears as an agent of Zeus' justice in Aeschylus 's tragic trilogy the Oresteia. In Agamemnon, the first play of the trilogy, Ate is linked with Helen of Troy, and Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra, both of whom act as agents of Zeus' retribution.

wiki_only_topics.topic: The landing place of Ate in Phrygia and the founding of Troy
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: According to the mythographer Apollodorus, when Ate was thrown down by Zeus, Ate landed in Phrygia at a place called "the hill of the Phrygian Ate", where the city of Troy was founded.

wiki_only_topics.topic: Ate as an agent of Zeus' divine retribution and justice
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: Ate (or the impersonal atē) is often referred to as the agent (or instrument) of Zeus' divine retribution. In the Iliad, Zeus is begged to send Ate so that the denier of "Prayers... may fall and pay full recompense."
